questions.subject: English
questions.stem:
No one is born hating another person because of
the colour of his skin, or his background, or his
religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can
learn to hate, they can be taught to love, for love
comes more naturally to the human heart than its
opposite. Even in the grimmest times in prison, when
my comrades and I were pushed to our limits, I would
see a glimmer of humanity in one of the guards,
perhaps just for a second, but it was enough to
reassure me and keep me going. Man’s goodness is
a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.

While preparing for a comprehension test, a student must note the single idea that the extract shows, so which of these notes fits it best? (A) People are born hating one another because of the colour of their skin. (B) Even in the cruelest conditions, a small spark of human goodness is enough to keep a person going. (C) Learning to hate comes more naturally to the human heart than learning to love. (D) Human goodness is completely destroyed by years in prison.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Even in the cruelest conditions, a small spark of human goodness is enough to keep a person going.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: A student has to join two closely related statements into a single sentence: "Freedom is indivisible" and "the chains on anyone of my people were the chains on all of them". Which punctuation mark, and what treatment of the word "the", does the rule require? (A) a full stop, with "The" in capital letters (B) a colon, with "the" in small letters (C) a semi-colon, with "the" in small letters (D) a dash, with "the" in small letters

answerScheme.modelAnswer: a semi-colon, with "the" in small letters

evidence:
Freedom is indivisible; the chains on anyone of
my people were the chains on all of them, the
chains on all of my people were the chains on me.

options.A: a full stop, with "The" in capital letters
options.B: a colon, with "the" in small letters
options.C: a semi-colon, with "the" in small letters
options.D: a dash, with "the" in small letters

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write a letter to the Principal of your school in about 100 words, suggesting that the school's Freedom Day programme should speak not only about the end of a political system but also about freedom from poverty, deprivation and all forms of discrimination.

markingPoints.description: Content: the letter asks for freedom from poverty, deprivation and all forms of discrimination to be included, and not only the end of a political system.
Format: it is written as a formal letter, with the correct form of address, a salutation and a closing.
Organisation: the ideas run in a clear order, from the reason for the request to the request itself.
Accuracy: correct grammar, spelling and punctuation throughout.
Expression: a polite tone and a vocabulary suited to a student writing to the Principal, in about 100 words.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Dear Principal, I wish to suggest a change in our Freedom Day programme. At present it speaks only about the end of a political system. But freedom is not complete while people still live in poverty and deprivation, or are treated differently because of their gender or race. I therefore ask you to add a short talk on freedom from all forms of discrimination, so that students learn that a nation can win political emancipation and still have work to do. This will make the programme meaningful for students who see such unfairness around them. Yours obediently, A Student.

evidence:
We have, at last, achieved our political emancipation.
We pledge ourselves to liberate all our people from the
continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering,
gender and other discrimination.

in a country like South Africa, it was almost
impossible for a man of my birth and colour to fulfil
both of those obligations. In South Africa, a man of
colour who attempted to live as a human being was
punished and isolated.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write a speech of about 100 words to be delivered in your school assembly on the topic "True liberty is freedom from poverty, deprivation and all forms of discrimination". Make brief notes in writing before you write the speech.

markingPoints.description: Content: the speech explains that liberty means freedom from poverty, deprivation and all forms of discrimination, and not only political freedom.
Format: it is written as a speech, opening with a greeting and closing with a thank you to the audience.
Organisation: brief notes in writing come first, and the points of the speech then follow in a clear order.
Accuracy: correct grammar, spelling and punctuation, in sentences that can be spoken aloud.
Expression: a vocabulary and tone suited to a school assembly, in about 100 words.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Good morning, everyone. A country can win its political emancipation and still leave many of its people in poverty and deprivation. Nelson Mandela pledged to liberate all his people from the continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination. So true liberty means freedom from all of these, and not from one political system alone. I ask each of us to look for one small unfairness in our own school and to speak against it. Let freedom reign. Thank you.

evidence:

continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering,
gender and other discrimination.

In a literature class, a student is asked what the image of the sun in this extract suggests about the achievement the speaker describes, and which answer is best? (A) The speaker believes the country will soon return to its earlier rulers. (B) The speaker believes the achievement belongs only to one race of people. (C) The speaker believes the sun itself will always be seen in the country. (D) The speaker believes the achievement will outlast the moment and remain a lasting glory.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The speaker believes the achievement will outlast the moment and remain a lasting glory.

achievement.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: On the day of the inauguration whites sang one national anthem and blacks sang another. Why did Mandela say that the playing of the two anthems symbolised the day for him?

markingPoints.description: Whites sang Nkosi Sikelel -i Afrika and blacks sang Die Stem.
Each group had once despised the anthem of the other group.
The two groups singing together showed that blacks and whites now shared one country.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: One anthem, Nkosi Sikelel -i Afrika, was sung by whites and the other, Die Stem, by blacks. Each group had once despised the anthem of the other and did not know its words. As the two were played, and both groups were soon to know the words by heart, the day stood for blacks and whites sharing one country.

evidence:
The day was symbolised for me by the playing of
our two national anthems, and the vision of whites
singing ‘Nkosi Sikelel –iAfrika’ and blacks singing
‘Die Stem’, the old anthem of the Republic.

that day neither group knew the lyrics of the anthem
they once despised, they would soon know the
words by heart.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Mandela says that the brave man is not he who does not feel afraid. In what way, then, does he define courage, and from whom did he learn it?

markingPoints.description: Courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it.
The brave man is the one who conquers that fear, not the one who never feels it.
He learned it from comrades in the struggle who risked their lives for an idea and stood up to attacks and torture without breaking.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Courage, Mandela says, is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it, and the brave man is the one who conquers that fear. He learned this meaning from his comrades in the struggle, men and women who risked and gave their lives for an idea and stood up to attacks and torture without breaking.

evidence:
that courage was not the absence of fear, but the
triumph over it. The brave man is not he who does
not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.

It is from these comrades in the struggle that I
learned the meaning of courage. Time and again, I
have seen men and women risk and give their lives
for an idea.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: The ceremonies at the inauguration were held in the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria. What did that place stand for earlier, and what did it stand for on the day of the inauguration?

markingPoints.description: For decades the amphitheatre had been the seat of white supremacy.
On the day of the inauguration it became the site of a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations.
There South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government was installed.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria had been, for decades, the seat of white supremacy. On the day of the inauguration the same site became a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations, gathered there for the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government.

evidence:
The ceremonies took place in the lovely
sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union
Buildings in Pretoria. For decades this had been
the seat of white supremacy, and now it was the
site of a rainbow gathering of different colours and
nations for the installation of South Africa’s first
democratic, non-racial government.

questions.subject: English
questions.topic: Twin Obligations and the Meaning of Freedom
questions.stem: Mandela says that in a civil and humane society every man is able to fulfil his twin obligations. Why did he find it almost impossible to do so in South Africa?

markingPoints.description: In a civil and humane society each man is able to fulfil both obligations, to his family and to his people.
In South Africa, however, it was almost impossible for a man of birth and colour to fulfil both of those obligations.
A man of colour who attempted to live as a human being was punished and isolated.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: In a civil and humane society a man is able to fulfil both those obligations, to his family and to his people, according to his own inclinations and abilities. In South Africa, however, it was almost impossible for a man to fulfil both, because a man of colour who attempted to live as a human being was punished and isolated.

evidence:
In life, every man has twin obligations —
obligations to his family, to his parents, to his wife
and children; and he has an obligation to his people,
his community, his country. In a civil and humane
society, each man is able to fulfil those obligations
according to his own inclinations and abilities.

in a country like South Africa, it was almost
impossible for a man of my birth and colour to fulfil
both of those obligations. In South Africa, a man of
colour who attempted to live as a human being was
punished and isolated.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: In about 120 words, and step by step, set out the changes that the day of the inauguration itself showed in South Africa, using what Nelson Mandela says about that day.

markingPoints.description: For decades the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria had been the seat of white supremacy.
On the day of the inauguration it became the site of a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations.
South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government was installed there.
Outlaws were now allowed to host the nations of the world on their own soil.
Whites and blacks each sang the anthem that the other group had once despised.
A chevron of Impala jets drew the black, red, green, blue and gold of the new flag in the shape of a V.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1 - For decades the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria had been the seat of white supremacy. Step 2 - On the day of the inauguration it became the site of a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations. Step 3 - It was there for the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government. Step 4 - Outlaws were now allowed to host the nations of the world on their own soil. Step 5 - Whites sang Nkosi Sikelel -i Afrika and blacks sang Die Stem, the two anthems each group had once despised. Step 6 - A chevron of Impala jets drew the black, red, green, blue and gold of the new flag in a V.

Buildings in Pretoria. For decades this had been

site of a rainbow gathering of different colours and
nations for the installation of South Africa’s first
democratic, non-racial government.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Mandela writes that it requires such depths of oppression to create such heights of character. In about 120 words, and step by step, show how the decades of oppression and brutality produced both a lasting wound in his country and character of rare quality in its people.

markingPoints.description: Apartheid was a political system that separated people according to their race.
It created a deep and lasting wound from which all will spend years, if not generations, recovering.
It produced the Oliver Tambos, the Walter Sisulus, the Chief Luthulis, the Yusuf Dadoos, the Bram Fischers and the Robert Sobukwes.
Their courage, wisdom and generosity were such that their like may never be known again.
It also produced comrades who risked and gave their lives for an idea and stood up to attacks and torture without breaking.
From such comrades Mandela learned that courage is the triumph over fear, not its absence.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1 - Apartheid was a political system that separated people according to their race. Step 2 - It created a deep and lasting wound in the country and its people, from which all will spend years, if not generations, recovering. Step 3 - Yet it also produced the Oliver Tambos, the Walter Sisulus, the Chief Luthulis, the Yusuf Dadoos, the Bram Fischers, the Robert Sobukwes. Step 4 - Their courage, wisdom and generosity were such that their like may never be known again. Step 5 - It produced comrades who risked and gave their lives for an idea and stood up to attacks and torture without breaking. Step 6 - From them Mandela learned that courage is the triumph over fear, not its absence.

wound in my country and my people. All of us will
spend many years, if not generations, recovering
from that profound hurt.
